answer: Replaying a $50,000, 10-year private loan over every 120-month window of 3-month T-bill history since 1954 (753 start months), a variable rate that starts at 7.5% and moves one-for-one with the bill rate ended up costing more in total interest than a 9% fixed rate in 14.2% of windows. The median window had the variable loan $3,832 cheaper (fixed-rate interest: $26,005). But the losses were concentrated: 28.4% of windows starting 1954-1980 cost more versus 3.5% starting 1981 or later, and the worst window (starting 1977-04) cost $11,219 more, with the variable rate in that window peaking at 19.26%. The highest variable rate in any window was 20.6% (window starting 1972-02). History, not a forecast.
guess: A grad student would likely guess a variable loan is a coin flip or worse over 10 years, since rates can rise, and that a 1.5-point head start is easily wiped out.
changesDecision: The head start was overturned in a small minority of windows overall, but far more often in windows in the rising-rate decades before 1981, and the downside was large (up to $11,219 extra on $50,000). The decision becomes a question of which kind of history the borrower wants to be protected against, not a rule of thumb.

assumptions: Offers taken as given: 9.00% fixed and 7.50% variable at origination; the variable loan reprices monthly as a fixed margin plus the 3-month T-bill rate (proxy for the SOFR or similar index lenders use).
Index path = today's T-bill level (3.72) plus the historical change since the start month, floored at zero; no rate cap.
Repayment starts immediately, 120 level payments re-amortized when the rate changes; no in-school deferment, fees, autopay discounts, prepayment or default.
Start months 1954-01 onward (after the 1951 Treasury-Fed accord ended the wartime yield peg).
limits: History, not a forecast. Overlapping 10-year windows are not independent; the sample has essentially two regimes (rising 1954-1981, falling 1981-2021). Real private loans may cap the rate, use a different index or margin, and price by credit score.
